clue.text: Manage group in tennis gear

blocks.note: to head a department is to manage it
a band is a group, of musicians or of anyone else

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are office words on the surface — one runs a department, the other plays music — and only when they are read as one word does anything sporting appear.
explanation.definitionFit: tennis gear: definition by example, since the answer is one item of a player's kit, the strip that keeps sweat and hair out of the eyes.

clue.text: Admonisher, after massage, is reconciled

indicators.note: Massage is kneading something into a new shape, so what comes out of it is not in the order it went in.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder — a scolder, the person who tells you off

explanation.walkthrough: Ten letters is a lot to shuffle blind, so the tell is the surface: a scolder having a massage is a sentence built to be taken apart, not believed.
explanation.definitionFit: reconciled: voices harmonised are brought into agreement, and the musical picture is how English says a quarrel has been settled.

clue.text: We're known to be bent in the workplace and when we're not charged, you're in the dark

definitions.text: We're known to be bent in the workplace and when we're not charged, you're in the dark

blocks.clueFragment: We're known to be bent in the workplace
blocks.note: the surface accuses a pair of crooked office workers; read straight, being bent is the whole point of a jointed arm on a desk

blocks.clueFragment: when we're not charged, you're in the dark
blocks.note: 'charged' sits next to 'bent' so it reads as a police charge, and the darkness gives the real sense away: no power, no light

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to take apart. The first person plural is the objects talking, which turns 'we're bent' into a boast about design rather than a confession.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is one description: a desk lamp made to be bent into position, and useless the moment its power is cut.

clue.text: I'll give you energy: like a pancake?

definitions.note: The answer is a thing, but the setter lets it speak: 'I'll give you energy' says what it does for you rather than offering a noun you could swap in.

blocks.note: a pancake is nothing but batter until it hits the pan
the -y ending English adds to mean 'resembling it': sugary, watery, chalky

explanation.walkthrough: The colon does the work of an equals sign, and the question mark is the setter admitting that the second half is a made-up adjective rather than a word you would find in a dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: I'll give you energy: the cell stores charge and hands it over on demand, so the clue names the thing purely by its one job.

clue.text: Chip's the ultimate in he-men, virile, topless

indicators.note: The ultimate one is the last one, and 'in' points at the phrase that follows: take only its final letter.
This is a down clue, so the top of a word is the letter at its head, and a topless word has lost it.

blocks.note: the letter at the very end of the hyphenated phrase
virile is macho, and that word beheaded leaves four letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chip's' looks possessive and is really 'chip is', which is the join between definition and wordplay. The crisp on the plate has nothing to do with the muscle-bound surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Chip: the clue names the class and leaves you to supply the Mexican member of it, a single triangle of fried tortilla.

clue.text: Fighting a dermal disorder after cycling

indicators.note: Cycling sends a letter round from one end of a word to the other with the rest keeping their order; the bike ride is decoration.

blocks.note: the article taken at face value, one letter
a wart is a blemish of the skin, and its last letter rides round to the front

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a cyclist with a skin complaint; the answer is two words about armies. 'Dermal' is there to say which kind of blemish is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Fighting: the phrase describes two sides in open conflict, so it stands in wherever you could say that nations are fighting.

clue.text: Country song about chess pieces

indicators.note: Something placed about another thing is wrapped round the outside of it, so what follows goes inside.

blocks.note: an aria is the song a character sings in an opera
the pieces on a board are collectively its men

explanation.walkthrough: The surface promises country and western; the definition means country in the atlas sense. Chess supplying MEN is a convention worth pocketing — it turns up constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Country: the clue names the category and the answer supplies one particular member of it, the small republic south of the Caucasus.

clue.text: They're inclined to get you to leave

definitions.text: They're inclined to get you to leave

blocks.note: the surface reads this as 'disposed to'; the sense meant is the physical one, sloping rather than willing
not a hint to clear off — it is about being able to get out of a building at all

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here is spelled out of anything. The clue turns on one word carrying two senses at once, which is the whole of what a cryptic definition asks you to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes the sloped runs that let a wheeled user get out of a building — inclined meaning tilted, not willing.

clue.text: Looking up, I'll add: a glimpse of rank and file

indicators.note: This is a down clue, so anything looking up is read from the bottom of the grid towards the top — backwards, in other words.
You catch only the beginning of something you glimpse, so take the opening letter of the word that follows.

blocks.note: a postscript is what you add after signing off
the article standing as one letter
the opening letter of the word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank and file' is one phrase on the surface and two jobs underneath: only 'rank' feeds the wordplay, and 'file' is the definition sitting at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: file: a rasp is the coarse-toothed file a woodworker reaches for when the shaping is still rough, so the definition is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Romantic German in school, increasingly unwell

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation, as printed on a map or a timetable
'increasingly' asks for the comparative — more ill than before

explanation.walkthrough: The capital R is the clue's one piece of honesty: this is the literary movement, not a lovestruck tourist, and the man wanted is its poet and playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Romantic German: definition by example — he is one particular writer of German Romanticism, and the capital letter flags the movement rather than a mood.

clue.text: Booked man of many words

definitions.note: 'Booked' is a participle where the answer is a person's surname: the setter means his words ended up between covers, so the grammar bends for the joke.

blocks.note: the surface offers cautioned or reserved; the sense wanted is that the name now sits on a spine on every reference shelf
the Victorian physician who spent his retirement listing synonyms by the thousand

explanation.walkthrough: The thesaurus is so completely his that the surname alone has come to mean the book, and that is exactly what 'Booked' is playing on.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves point at Peter Mark Roget: the doctor who compiled a thesaurus of synonyms, and whose surname has since become the book itself.

clue.text: Before seconds, alternately crunch on brown salad components

indicators.note: The word says where the last piece sits: everything else has to be assembled in front of it.
Taking a word alternately means keeping every other letter and throwing away the ones in between.

blocks.note: every other letter of the word, starting at the first
umber is a brown earth pigment, raw or burnt
s is the abbreviation on any stopwatch

explanation.walkthrough: Everything on the surface is edible, and only 'brown' is doing colour work: umber is a painter's pigment rather than a food, which is the switch the clue turns on.
explanation.definitionFit: salad components: the plural names them as one of the handful of vegetables a green salad gets sliced together from.

clue.text: Into amore ('love') - badly so?

indicators.note: Doing a thing badly is doing it wrong, and letters put together wrong are letters put together in the wrong order.

blocks.note: thirteen letters of fodder, the bracketed translation counted in

explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is not an aside: the glossed word is fodder too. And the sentence doubles as the definition, which is what an all-in-one clue does.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight the clue defines itself: being badly into romance means feelings pitched far higher than the occasion asks for.

clue.text: Nicer day in resort: very hot

indicators.note: Split it as re-sort and the holiday town becomes an instruction: put these letters in order a second time.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, holiday brochure and all

explanation.walkthrough: 'Very hot' is not about the weather the surface is selling: the answer is the word for a remark inflammatory enough to set a room alight.
explanation.definitionFit: very hot: literally fire-raising, and used of anything — a speech, a report — heated enough to start something burning.

clue.text: Tough guy finally getting subtle humour

indicators.note: The word points at the end of whatever precedes it, so only that word's closing letter is wanted.

blocks.note: iron stands for anything hard and unyielding — an iron will, an iron constitution
the last letter of the word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tough guy' is one idea on the surface and two separate instructions underneath, which is the whole trick of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: subtle humour: saying the opposite of what you mean and trusting your listener to hear it — comedy that never announces itself.

clue.text: What is unusual and concerning about a 50k race no-one runs?

indicators.note: Something unusual is out of its ordinary state, and for a word that means out of its ordinary order.
One piece placed about another goes round the outside of it, so what follows drops inside.

blocks.note: the four letters of the question word, re-ordered
a, then L for the Roman fifty, then k
on means concerning, as in a book on birds

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark concedes that the definition is a joke, and the distance is not measuring anything: '50k' is there to hand over three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: race no-one runs: a sponsored long-distance walk is a race by courtesy only, since the point of it is that nobody breaks into a run.

clue.text: Some raw earth I neglected to grow ragged

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole of it, which is where the letters are sitting.

blocks.note: the letters run unbroken through these words, starting partway into the first

explanation.walkthrough: A long hidden answer hides best behind a plausible sentence, and this one runs straight through a gardener's excuse. 'Some' is the only signpost you are given.
explanation.definitionFit: grow ragged: cloth rubbed until it is nearly through, and by extension a joke or a patience that is close to giving out.

clue.text: Laid-back committee head, one comfortably supporting you

blocks.note: a laid-back person is unhurried and untroubled
whoever chairs a meeting is simply the chair

explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes furniture but reads as a person, which is what keeps the committee surface standing up right to the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: one comfortably supporting you: the definition names the armchair by what it does, taking your weight in padded comfort.

clue.text: In America, GI esteemed as 'most sly'

indicators.note: 'In' says the letters are already sitting inside the words that follow and need no assembling.

blocks.note: the letters run on across the end of one word and into the next two

explanation.walkthrough: The comma and the capital letters are all working for the surface, which is precisely where the eye stops looking for a join.
explanation.definitionFit: most sly: cagey means wary and unwilling to give anything away, so the superlative is guardedness rather than outright cunning.

clue.text: Pull up fish escaping from trap

indicators.note: A trap is British slang for the mouth, so whatever escapes from one is spoken rather than written down.

blocks.note: rays are the flat cartilaginous sea fish, and 'fish' serves as its own plural

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sells a fish wriggling out of a fish trap, which sets you hunting for a deletion. Nothing is taken away here: the clue only asks you to say the word aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Pull up: a plain synonym in the lifting sense — you pull up a blind, or pull up a bucket from a well, and that is the movement wanted.

clue.text: Most of greens, sadly, Everyman's eaten for diet

indicators.note: Taking most of a word means keeping all of it but the final letter.
Sadly here means badly, out of sorts — and letters out of sorts are letters out of order.
What is eaten disappears inside the eater, which is where these two letters go.

blocks.note: drop the last letter of the vegetables and re-order the five that are left
the setter calls himself Everyman, so 'Everyman is' shortens to I'm

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signs his own puzzles: whenever his name appears it means I or me, and it is worth learning because he uses it most weeks.
explanation.definitionFit: diet: a regimen is the whole prescribed routine of food, rest and exercise, and 'diet' names the eating half of it.

clue.text: Disorder persisted - Spooner's inclined to steal

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner traded the opening sounds of two words, so naming him is the instruction to swap them over.

blocks.note: a fight is disorder breaking out
what persisted has lingered on
say those two words with their opening sounds traded, F for L

explanation.walkthrough: A Spooner clue is easiest attacked from the definition end: think of the phrase for a thief first, then swap the sounds back and check the clue's own words appear.
explanation.definitionFit: inclined to steal: the idiom names a habitual petty thief by the deftness of the hands that do the taking.

clue.text: Leading characters in Irish netball won gold?

indicators.note: A word's leading character is the letter it starts with, and 'in' points at which words to take them from.

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the two words
you got the prize you won

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter admitting that the bar need not be gold — silver and steel are cast the same way — while the surface keeps you on medals.
explanation.definitionFit: gold: definition by example, since the answer is a cast bar of any metal and the bar everyone pictures happens to be the bullion one.

clue.text: Estonian regularly ignored volcano

indicators.note: The letters in the regular positions are the ones thrown away, leaving every other one behind.

blocks.note: drop every second letter of the nationality and read what is left

explanation.walkthrough: An eight-letter nationality and a four-letter answer: the arithmetic tells you letters are being discarded before you have worked out which ones.
explanation.definitionFit: volcano: definition by example — the answer is one particular Sicilian mountain, and the clue names only the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Softening but hardening

blocks.note: moderating something — taking the edge off a remark, a mood or a judgement
the smith's heat-and-quench treatment that toughens steel

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, and the middle one pretends to object. The contradiction is the clue: one word is used in opposite directions by moralists and metalworkers.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word runs both ways: moderating a mood takes the heat out of it, while the heat treatment leaves steel harder than it was.

clue.text: Primarily mouthy African menace biting avians?

definitions.text: Primarily mouthy African menace biting avians?

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of each following word counts.

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the five words, read in order

explanation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs: it hands over a letter and it describes the creature. The question mark covers the birds, which are a snack rather than a speciality.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight the clue describes the snake itself: a fast African killer that strikes with its mouth and does take birds.

clue.text: Hound having chased away bishop: that's useful

definitions.note: The answer is a noun and 'useful' an adjective; the setter's 'that's' does the joining, leaving you to supply the thing that is useful.

indicators.note: Whatever a hound drives off is gone, so the letter named after it comes out of the word in front.

blocks.note: a basset is a short-legged breed of hound
b is the bishop in chess notation

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a dog chasing a clergyman. The wordplay wants the breed rather than the animal, and the chessboard supplies the letter that leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: useful: an asset is anything on the credit side, a resource you are glad to have, so the accountant's sense widens into any advantage.

clue.text: Supports - without doing anything?

blocks.note: staying loyal to someone through trouble, refusing to move away from them
waiting in readiness, or simply looking on while something happens

explanation.walkthrough: The dash is doing the work of 'or', and the question mark flags the unflattering reading: the same phrase praises a friend and condemns a bystander.
explanation.definitionFit: One phrase, two attitudes: backing a friend through trouble, and looking on while something happens without lifting a finger.
